rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God did not adopt anyone as a child; this rebuts Quraysh, Christians, and Jews who ascribe offspring to Him.
rows.anchor: الظاهر نفي الاتخاذ أي لم ينزل أحدا منزلة الولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative says God has no child, as in “He did not beget,” since procreation is impossible for Him.
rows.anchor: لم يكن له ولد بمعنى قوله لم يلد لأن التوالد مستحيل عليه

words: وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُۥ شَرِيكٌۭ فِى ٱلْمُلْكِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial of a partner reinforces God's ownership of heaven and earth and rejects those who assign Him one.
rows.anchor: تأكيد لقوله له ملك السماوات والأرض ورد على من جعل لله شريكا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Everything” is general, encompassing created entities and their actions.
rows.anchor: وخلق كل شيء عام في خلق الذوات وأفعالها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One proposed an omitted qualification, “everything whose creation is valid,” to exclude God's essence and eternal attributes.
rows.anchor: وفي الكلام حذف تقديره وخلق كل شيء مما يصح خلقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No qualification is needed: “I honored every man” does not include the speaker, just as this universal excludes God and His eternal attributes.
rows.anchor: ولا يحتاج إلى هذا المحذوف لأن من قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If creation means measuring, “then He measured it” risks repeating the same meaning.
rows.anchor: إن كان الخلق بمعنى التقدير

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says God brought each thing into existence in due proportion and prepared it for what suits it.
rows.anchor: فقال الزمخشري: المعنى أنه أحدث كل شيء إحداثا مراعى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Alternatively, God's wise creation brings each thing into existence according to a measure, without disparity.
rows.anchor: إلا على وجه التقدير من غير تفاوت

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Another explanation treats “created” as simply produced, then measured in its coming to be.
rows.anchor: وأوجد كل شيء فقدره في إيجاده متفاوتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says God assigned each thing an endpoint, measuring its persistence to a known term.
rows.anchor: فجعل له غاية ومنتهى

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya defines measuring things by place, time, quantity, benefit, and precision.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: تقدير الأشياء هو حدها بالأمكنة والأزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers to people inferred from the preceding denials, which answer claims made against God.
rows.anchor: الضمير في واتخذوا عائد على ما يفهم من سياق الكلام

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmānī identifies the subject as the unbelievers, included in “to the worlds.”
rows.anchor: وقال الكرماني: الواو ضمير للكفار وهم مندرجون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view infers the subject from “a warner,” since the people warned are those meant by “they.”
rows.anchor: لفظ نذيرا ينبئ عنهم لأنهم المنذرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording includes all who claim a deity besides God, not only idol or celestial-body worshippers.
rows.anchor: ويندرج في واتخذوا كل من ادعى إلها غير الله

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The Qāḍī doubts Christians are included because they did not take multiple gods; he favors idol worshippers but allows angel worshippers.
rows.anchor: وقال القاضي: يبعد أن يدخل فيه النصارى لأنهم لم يتخذوا من دون الله آلهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Plural wording need not match a collective plural referent, so Christians' object of worship can be included under “gods.”
rows.anchor: ولا يلزم ما قال لأن واتخذوا جمع وآلهة جمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Fables of the ancients” may be predicate of an omitted subject, or subject with “he had them written” as predicate.
rows.anchor: وأساطير الأولين خبر مبتدأ محذوف أي هو أو هذه أساطير

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read the verb actively.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور اكتتبها مبنيا للفاعل

rows.speaker: طلحة
rows.claim: Ṭalḥa reads the verb passively.
rows.anchor: وقراءة طلحة مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains the passive as a scribe writing tales for the unlettered Prophet, part of his inimitability.
rows.anchor: وهو من كلام الزمخشري ولا يصح ذلك على مذهب جمهور البصريين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects al-Zamakhsharī's analysis under mainstream Basran grammar: the construction has two objects, so passivization should yield another form.
rows.anchor: ولا يصح ذلك على مذهب جمهور البصريين لأن اكتتبها له كاتب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq's line supports the rule that the direct object alone becomes subject in the passive.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر وهو الفرزدق: ومنا الذي اختير الرجال سماحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent reading makes dictation morning and evening part of the unbelievers' accusation.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله اكتتبها فهي تملى عليه بكرة وأصيلا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan takes it as God's exposure of their lie; this works only with an interrogative hamza of repudiation.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن أنه قول الله سبحانه بكذبهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan should stop reciting at “the ancients.”
rows.anchor: وحق للحسن أن يقف على الأولين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Morning and evening may mean when people disperse and return home, or signify continual dictation.
rows.anchor: والظهر تقييد الإملاء بوقت انتشار الناس

rows.speaker: طلحة وعيسى
rows.claim: Ṭalḥa and ʿĪsā read “tutlā” (recited) with tāʾ instead of mīm.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة وعيسى فهي تتلى بالتاء بدل الميم

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says their analogies are pointless: unable to challenge the Prophet's miracles, the unbelievers resort to irrelevant talk.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله الرازي انظر كيف اشتغل القوم بضرب هذه الأمثال

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says they cannot find a stratagem in the Prophet's case.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: لا يستطيعون في أمرك حيلة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī explains the phrase as no path to attack or criticize the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي سبيلا إلى الطعن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anonymous report says the Prophet was offered worldly treasuries or equivalent reward in the afterlife; he chose to receive it there, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: إن شئت أن نعطيك خزائن الدنيا ومفاتيحها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Gabriel offered Mecca's plain as gold; the Prophet chose satiety one day and hunger three for remembrance and supplication.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس عنه عليه السلام قال: عرض على جبريل عليه السلام بطحاء مكة ذهبا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī glosses “tabāraka” as abundant in goodness and says God could give more in this life than the unbelievers proposed.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري في تبارك أي تكاثر خيرا الذي إن شاء وهب لك في الدنيا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says “that” refers to the unbelievers' mention of paradise and treasure in this world.
rows.anchor: والإشارة بذلك الظاهر أنه إلى ما ذكره الكفار من الجنة والكنز في الدنيا قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The author considers Ibn ʿAbbās's proposed referent—the Prophet eating and walking in markets—unlikely.
rows.anchor: ويبعد تأويل ابن عباس أنه إشارة إلى أكله الطعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent promise concerns a worldly grant if God wills; another view places it in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن هذا الجعل كان يكون في الدنيا لو شاءه الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional signals dependence on divine grace and will; no servant has a claim on God in either life.
rows.anchor: لا ينال ذلك إلا برحمته وأنه معلق على محض مشيئته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worldly interpretation better rebukes the unbelievers.
rows.anchor: والأول أبلغ في تبكيت الكفار والرد عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the next clause refutes the referent; the author says it adds their denial of the Hour as a worse offense.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ويرده قوله بعد ذلك بل كذبوا بالساعة

rows.speaker: نافع، حمزة، الكسائي، أبو عمرو
rows.claim: These readers recite the verb jussively, coordinated with the implied conditional “makes.”
rows.anchor: والذي قرأ بالجزم من السبعة نافع وحمزة والكسائي وأبو عمرو

rows.speaker: مجاهد، ابن عامر، ابن كثير، حميد، أبو بكر، محبوب عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: These authorities read the verb in the indicative; Ibn ʿAṭiyya links it to “makes,” while al-Ḥūfī treats it as independent.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد وابن عامر وابن كثير وحميد وأبو بكر ومحبوب عن أبي عمرو بالرفع

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ parses the indicative as an independent sentence.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء وبالرفع على الاستئناف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says an indicative response is possible after a past-tense conditional and cites poetry.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وقرئ ويجعل بالرفع عطفا على جعل

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh says the answer is omitted and the raised imperfect is intended to precede the conditional.
rows.anchor: مذهب سيبويه أن الجواب محذوف وأن هذا المضارع المرفوع النية به التقديم

rows.speaker: الكوفيون والمبرد
rows.claim: The Kufans and al-Mubarrad treat the imperfect as the answer with an omitted faʾ.
rows.anchor: وذهب الكوفيون والمبرد إلى أنه هو الجواب وأنه على حذف الفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis makes it the answer without omitted faʾ or fronting because the past-form conditional has little visible governing effect.
rows.anchor: وذهب غير هؤلاء إلى أنه هو الجواب وليس على حذف الفاء

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most grammarians regard this construction as eloquent and permissible in ordinary speech.
rows.anchor: وذهب الجمهور إلى أن هذا التركيب فصيح وأنه جائز في الكلام

rows.speaker: بعض أصحابنا
rows.claim: Some colleagues consider it poetic license, with implicit faʾ.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض أصحابنا: هو ضرورة إذ لم يجئ إلا في الشعر

rows.speaker: عبيد الله بن موسى، طلحة بن سليمان
rows.claim: They read the verb subjunctively with implicit “an”; Abū al-Fatḥ calls it a weak answer to the conditional with waw.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبيد الله بن موسى وطلحة بن سليمان ويجعل بالنصب

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nābigha's verse shows the verb in genitive, indicative, and subjunctive variants.
rows.anchor: ونظير هذه القراءات الثلاث قول النابغة

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmānī says denial of the Hour, not the Prophet's eating or walking in markets, prevents faith.
rows.anchor: قال الكرماني: المعنى ما منعهم من الإيمان أكلك الطعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says their complaints are no real objection; they reject the Hour because they dislike preparing for it.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ليس ما تعلقوا به شبهة بل الحامل على تكذيبك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another syntax links the clause to what follows: those denying the afterlife would not heed an answer or believe its reward.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يجوز أن يكون متصلا بما يليه كأنه قال بل كذبوا بالساعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Bal” shifts wording without cancelling the preceding meaning.
rows.anchor: وبل لترك اللفظ المتقدم من غير إبطال لمعناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Aʿtadnā” means “We prepared.”
rows.anchor: وأعتدنا جعلناه معدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Saʿīr” is a large, fiercely kindled fire.
rows.anchor: سعيرا نارا كبيرة الإيقاد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says Saʿīr is a name of Hell.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن: اسم من أسماء جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal reading is that Hell sees them; a report says it has two eyes, and if sound this is correct.
rows.anchor: قيل هو حقيقة وإن لجهنم عينين وروي في ذلك أثر فإن صح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Otherwise it is metaphor: Hell appears to extend toward them from afar, like houses facing one another.
rows.anchor: وإلا كان مجازا، أي صارت منهم بقدر ما يرى الرائي من البعد

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmānī reports a view that fire is a fiery creature able to speak, see, hear, move, and roar.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: النار اسم لحيوان ناري يتكلم ويرى ويسمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view supplies Hell's keepers as subject; reports set the distance at five hundred, one hundred, or one year.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو على حذف مضاف أي رأتهم خزنتها من مكان بعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since rage is not normally heard, keepers may be understood to rage and roar from anger and desire for vengeance.
rows.anchor: سمعوا لها صوت تغيظ لأن التغيظ لا يسمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes the sound as the fire's flames and crackling.
rows.anchor: وقيل سمعوا صوت لهيبها واشتعالها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry permits ellipsis or inclusive meaning; hearing may mean perceiving, and verbs may govern fitting sounds.
rows.anchor: فكذلك الآية أي سمعوا لها ورأوا تغيظا وزفيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Makānan” is an adverbial of place, meaning “in a narrow place.”
rows.anchor: وانتصب مكانا على الظرف أي في مكان ضيق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās compares the constriction to a spear socket.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: تضيق عليهم ضيق الزج في الرمح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says their hands are chained to their necks.
rows.anchor: مقرنين قرنت أيديهم إلى أعناقهم بالسلاسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says each unbeliever is chained to his devil, with shackles on their feet.
rows.anchor: يقرن مع كل كافر شيطانه في سلسلة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، عبيد عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr and ʿUbayd from Abū ʿAmr read “dayyiqan” instead of “dayqan.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وعبيد عن أبي عمر وضيقا

rows.speaker: أبو شيبة
rows.claim: Abū Shayba has an anomalous nominative reading attributed by Ibn Khālawayh to Muʿādh ibn Jabal.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو شيبة صاحب معاذ بن جبل مقرنون بالواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative may be appositive to the subject of “they were cast” or an accusative circumstantial.
rows.anchor: ووجهها أن يرتفع على البدل من ضمير ألقوا بدل نكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They cry “O destruction,” as if its time has come.
rows.anchor: والظاهر دعاء الثبور وهي الهلاك فيقولون: وا ثبوراه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation supplies an omitted object: they call on one who cannot answer, saying “destroy us.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: المدعو محذوف تقديره دعوا من لا يجيبهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses thubūr as woe.
rows.anchor: والثبور قال ابن عباس: هو الويل

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk glosses it as destruction; the author cites Ibn al-Zibaʿrā's poem.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: هو الهلاك ومنه قول ابن الزبعرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition may be spoken to them or narrated without a speaker; it means not to limit themselves to one cry because torment lasts or has many kinds.
rows.anchor: لا تدعوا اليوم يقال لهم لا تدعوا أو هم أحق أن يقال لهم ذلك

rows.speaker: عمرو بن محمد
rows.claim: ʿAmr ibn Muḥammad opens the thāʾ in three occurrences and the wāw in the verbal noun, a rare pattern.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمرو بن محمد ثبورا بفتح الثاء في ثلاثتها

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā explains “mā thabaraka” as what turned you away from the matter.
rows.anchor: وحكى علي بن عيسى: ما ثبرك عن هذا الأمر أي ما صرفك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anonymous report says Satan first cries “O destruction,” wears a garment from Hell and drags it behind; followers repeat him until keepers warn them.
rows.anchor: روي أن أول ما ينادي بذلك إبليس يقول: وا ثبوراه حتى يكسى حلة من جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent referent of “that” is the fire and the condition of its people.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الإشارة بذلك إلى النار وأحوال أهلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes it as paradise and treasure mentioned by the unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقيل إلى الجنة والكنز في قولهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view points to paradise and palaces that could be granted in this life if God willed.
rows.anchor: وقيل إلى الجنة والقصور المجعولة في الدنيا على تقدير المشيئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Better” need not rank the alternatives; Arab usage can use a comparative to single out virtue, as in poetry and proverb.
rows.anchor: وخير هنا ليست تدل على الأفضلية بل هي على ما جرت عادة العرب

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says a question can compare paradise and fire to test the interlocutor; Sībawayh's objection concerns declarations.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ومن حيث كان الكلام استفهاما جاز فيه مجيء لفظه للتفضيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cites declarative poetry and “prison is dearer to me” against the restriction, while allowing a declaration when superiority is obvious.
rows.anchor: وما ذكره يخالفه قوله: فشركما لخيركما الفداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted pronoun means “what they wish for”; this shows all desires are fulfilled only in paradise.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله ما يشاؤونه دليل على أن حصول المرادات بأسرها لا تكون إلا في

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Reward and final abode” includes recompense and its place; the resting place's quality magnifies bliss or punishment.
rows.anchor: وشمل قوله جزاء ومصيرا الثواب ومحله كما قال نعم الثواب وحسنت مرتفقا

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb says the promise is requested by angels praying for believers' admission to the gardens God promised.
rows.anchor: قاله محمد بن كعب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Zayd connect it to prayers for good promised through messengers in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: وقال معناه ابن عباس وابن زيد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says it means an assured obligation, like promising a thousand whether requested or not.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: وعدا مسؤلا أي واجبا يقال لأعطينك ألفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects calling al-Farrāʾ's interpretation impossible: the promise can be something that ought to be requested.
rows.anchor: ليس محالا إذ يكون المعنى أنه ينبغي أن يسأل هذا الوعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Upon your Lord” means His promise makes fulfillment certain.
rows.anchor: وعلى ربك أي بسبب الوعد صار لا بد منه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls fulfillment obligatory on God as deserved recompense; the author identifies this as Muʿtazilite doctrine.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: كان ذلك موعودا واجبا على ربك إنجازه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God taught the hoopoe to detect hidden water, it fittingly describes Him as bringing hidden things forth; specialist knowledge shows in manner and speech.
rows.anchor: كان الهدهد قد أوتي من معرفة الماء تحت الأرض ما لم يؤت غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says God clothes every servant with the mantle of the work he performs.
rows.anchor: ما عمل عبد عملا إلا ألقى الله عليه رداء عمله

rows.speaker: الحرميان والجمهور
rows.claim: The Ḥaramī readers and majority use third-person verbs referring to the queen and her people.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحرميان والجمهور: ما يخفون وما يعلنون

rows.speaker: الكسائي وحفص
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ use second-person address, possibly to Solomon and attendants.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكسائي وحفص: بتاء الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hoopoe could address Solomon's attendants too; it had already said it encompassed what Solomon did not.
rows.anchor: أحطت بما لم تحط به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent reading makes these words part of the hoopoe's speech.
rows.anchor: ألا يسجدوا إلى العظيم من كلام الهدهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes them as God's address to Muḥammad's community.
rows.anchor: من كلام الله تعالى لأمة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says third person indicates the hoopoe's speech and second person God's address.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: القراءة بياء الغيبة تعطي أن الآية من كلام الهدهد

rows.speaker: صاحب الغنيان
rows.claim: Al-Ghunyān's author says God responds to the hoopoe's praise of Bilqīs's throne: only God's throne merits true greatness.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب الغنيان: لما ذكر الهدهد عرش بلقيس ووصفه بالعظم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view treats this as the hoopoe redirecting greatness from Bilqīs's throne to God's.
rows.anchor: أنه من تمام كلام الهدهد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī distinguishes her throne's greatness among monarchs from God's throne's greatness relative to creation.
rows.anchor: كيف سوى الهدهد بين عرش بلقيس وعرش الله

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن وجماعة
rows.claim: They read the adjective nominatively, either describing the throne or as praise with implied “He is.”
rows.anchor: العظيم بالرفع، فاحتمل أن تكون صفة للعرش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative could instead modify “Lord”; the throne is singled out as greatest creation, with the rest subsumed.
rows.anchor: واحتمل أن تكون صفة للرب

none: The segment contains only the quoted verses 30:25-44, including 30:39, and no commentary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra is Meccan, though one view excepts five verses and Ibn ʿAbbās, Muqātil, and al-Kalbī except three Medinan verses.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية، قيل: إلا خمس آيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh said God had not sent Muḥammad and his message was fabricated; the verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: قال كفار قريش: لم يبعث الله محمدا إلينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the preceding sūra's proof of oneness through creation and resurrection, this one opens with prophethood.
rows.anchor: دلائل التوحيد من بدء الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After arguing from earlier nations destroyed for disbelief, God argues from displaying His power and alerting people to resurrection.
rows.anchor: فأهلكوا، ثم أقامها عليهم بإظهار قدرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As explained at 18:8, “al-jarz” is any barren land, not one specific place.
rows.anchor: وتقدم تفسير الجرز في الكهف، وكل أرض جزر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies it as Abyan in Yemen, watered by runoff rather than rain.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: هي أرض أبين من اليمن، وهي أرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant reads the rāʾ as quiescent.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: الجرز، بسكون الراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Through it” refers to water.
rows.anchor: فنخرج به: أي بالماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Crops are singled out though water produces useful plants because crops are honored and most important; “crop” stands for vegetation generally.
rows.anchor: وخص الزرع بالذكر، وإن كان يخرج الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Livestock come first because they eat growth as soon as it appears, before people eat grain and fodder is harvested.
rows.anchor: وقدمت الأنعام، لأن ما ينبت يأكله الأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reasons are that animals eat fodder while people have other foods, or that the verse moves from lower creatures to noble humans.
rows.anchor: أو لأنه غذاء الدواب، والإنسان قد يتغذى بغيره

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة، أبو بكر
rows.claim: They read the masculine singular “yaʾkulu.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة، وأبو بكر في رواية: يأكل

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read “yubṣirūn” in the third person.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: يبصرون، بياء الغيبة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads the closing question as direct address.
rows.anchor: وابن مسعود: بتاء الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The close suits a visible sign; the preceding verse concerns what is heard and asks whether they hear.
rows.anchor: وجاءت الفاصلة: أفلا يبصرون، لأن ما سبق مرئي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unbelievers mockingly demand that judgment between them and the Messenger be hastened.
rows.anchor: استعجال فصل القضاء بينهم وبين الرسول

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority understand “al-fatḥ” as judgment, fitting the next verse.
rows.anchor: الحكم، قاله الجمهور، وهو الذي يترتب عليه قوله

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid identify it as the conquest of Mecca, but converts' faith then would benefit them.
rows.anchor: ويضعف قول الحسن ومجاهد: فتح مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author likewise rejects identifying the day as Badr because it does not fit what follows.
rows.anchor: وكذا قول من قال: يوم بدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They will not be given respite means their punishment will not be delayed.
rows.anchor: ولا هم ينظرون: أي لا يؤخرون عن العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Day” is accusative with “will not benefit”: they reach the day, believe without benefit, and seek but receive no respite.
rows.anchor: فكأن قد حصلتم في ذلك اليوم وآمنتم، فلم ينفعكم الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to turn away and await victory over them.
rows.anchor: ثم أمر بالإعراض عنهم وانتظار النصر عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says they await victory over believers, as in “wait; we are waiting with you.”
rows.anchor: إنهم منتظرون للغلبة عليكم لقوله: فتربصوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says they await punishment though unaware of their fate.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنهم منتظرون العذاب، أي هذا حكمهم

rows.speaker: اليماني
rows.claim: The Yemeni reads the passive participle; the majority use the active form, awaiting their destruction.
rows.anchor: وقرأ اليماني: منتظرون، بفتح الظاء، اسم مفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the active reading, angels in heaven may await the unbelievers' inevitable destruction.
rows.anchor: فإن الملائكة في السماء ينتظرونه
